video_title: Stablecoins, Tokenization & the Future of Banking with Adam Nelson of FirstMark Capital
gist: FirstMark Capital fintech partner Adam Nelson argues stablecoins and tokenized real-world assets are a genuine platform shift on par with AI: ~$300B issued today versus a Treasury projection of $3T in five years, with Circle and Tether already earning bank-scale net income off treasury float. He maps where value accrues (issuer yield, enterprise distribution via portfolio companies Rain and Velocity, AI agents settling on stablecoin rails) and why incumbent bank and card-network moats are weaker than they look, while Dan Nathan presses on 24/7 tokenized equities, Hyperliquid's scale relative to Robinhood, and the Kalshi/Polymarket convergence into everything-apps.

themes.theme: Stablecoins as the live platform shift

insights.claim: Roughly $300 billion of stablecoins are issued today and stablecoin transaction volumes already exceed the Visa and Mastercard networks, which Adam Nelson frames as still a drop in the bucket rather than a mature market.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: A base rate to size the opportunity: if volume already tops the card networks at $300B of float, the payments TAM being contested is not speculative crypto but core money movement.
insights.quote: you're talking about $300 billion of of stable coins that are out in in uh in and issued. And you also have, you know, transaction volumes that are now kind of beyond the Visa and Mastercard networks

insights.claim: Legacy financial executives, not just founders, tell FirstMark that stablecoins and tokenized real-world assets will change the core of the financial system, and when asked what inning adoption is in they answer 'spring training' — i.e. the game has not started.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: If sober incumbents put adoption pre-inning-one, the repricing of payment and settlement infrastructure is a multi-year runway rather than a trade that is already crowded.
insights.quote: when I ask what inning are we in, they say we're in spring training

insights.claim: The unlock for stablecoins was regulatory: the Genius Act gave transparency into how stablecoins would be managed, which Nelson credits for the subsequent explosion of real use cases being built.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Regulatory clarity, not token prices, is the catalyst variable to track; follow-on legislation moves the value pools more than crypto market cap does.

insights.claim: Stablecoins are the first crypto product with a credible pitch to a non-crypto Fortune 100 CFO or bank — a dollar-pegged, treasury-backed instrument with 24/7 instant settlement at a fraction of traditional transaction cost — which is why the crypto-summer/crypto-winter framing no longer governs adoption.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Decouple stablecoin adoption from token price cycles when modeling it; the demand driver is enterprise cost-of-settlement, not speculation.
insights.quote: there's this currency that's uh pegged to the US dollar. It is backed by US treasuries and it can be used for 247 instant settlement with a fraction of the transaction costs that exist in the traditional financial system

insights.claim: Excluding stablecoins, Bitcoin and Ethereum together are worth less than $2 trillion — roughly Meta's market cap — which Dan Nathan uses to argue the tracked tokens are not that meaningful to the broader financial asset ecosystem and the story is really about the technology.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Argues against using BTC/ETH prices as the read on blockchain adoption; exposure to the theme may be better expressed through payments and infrastructure equities than tokens.
insights.quote: Bitcoin and Ethereum, they're less than $2 trillion in market cap, right? They're probably equivalent to that of, let's say, Meta's market cap

themes.theme: Incumbent moats: banks and the card networks

insights.claim: Adam Nelson believes the moats of too-big-to-fail banks are weaker than consensus assumes because money is the ultimate network-effect business and trust is migrating on-chain, forcing incumbents to innovate or bleed business.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to the durable-moat case for large-cap bank multiples; watch which institutions actually put core business on chain versus which only announce pilots.
insights.quote: I think the moes may be uh weaker than we think.

insights.claim: The most forward-thinking banks will pass stablecoin-driven settlement efficiency through to customers rather than defend fee income from friction, shifting their business model toward monetizing expertise and access.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Implies fee-line compression at institutions whose revenue depends on payment friction, and a re-rating toward advisory/balance-sheet-driven earnings quality.
insights.quote: they don't want to make money on friction. They want to make money on their expertise and their access

insights.claim: Visa and Mastercard's vulnerability is cost, not speed: their pitch to merchants is instant guarantee and ubiquity, so the pressure point is the expense of the system rather than settlement latency.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Reframes the bear case on the networks — model interchange and cost structure, not settlement time, as the disruption vector.
insights.quote: I think the bigger issue is the expensive not slow

insights.claim: The card networks' near-term prize from stablecoins is freeing capital locked up in prefunding requirements on both merchant and issuer sides, which they can then redeploy around the payment rather than in it.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Suggests stablecoin adoption is working-capital accretive for the networks near term, softening the disruption narrative for their equity.

insights.claim: Visa and Mastercard will not give up interchange fees — Nelson calls interchange the price of admission — and will instead use stablecoin infrastructure to improve cost structure and merchant/customer experience.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Interchange compression is the wrong short thesis on the networks; margin expansion via lower operating cost is the more likely outcome.
insights.quote: Now, do I think they're going to get rid of their interchange fees? Absolutely not. That's uh I think that's price of admission

insights.claim: Consumer inertia, not product quality, is what protects incumbent banks: NPS scores are mediocre and everyone complains, but customers do not move, so challengers win by bleeding away direct deposit and bill payments incrementally rather than by conversion events.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The metric to track for fintech share gain is direct-deposit and primary-account migration, not app downloads or funded accounts.
insights.quote: these have mediocre MPS, but people don't move

themes.theme: Issuer economics and the fight over on-chain yield

insights.claim: Circle and Tether, the two major stablecoin issuers, together would rank as roughly the eighth largest US bank by net income based on Nelson's math from a couple of months prior.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Quantifies why every incumbent is launching a coin — issuer float economics already rival top-ten bank earnings without the credit book.
insights.quote: I think that like together they would have been the eighth largest bank in the US in terms of net income

insights.claim: Stablecoin issuers monetize by treating user balances as float — effectively a checking account — and pushing the reserves into treasuries to capture the spread, which is the core reason so many stablecoins are being launched.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Issuer earnings are a levered bet on front-end rates; a cutting cycle compresses the entire profit pool driving today's stablecoin launches.
insights.quote: they're playing with your float while your money is in stable coins, which are effectively like your cash, your checking account, and they're pushing everything into uh into treasury and taking the spread

insights.claim: Whether yield can be paid on-chain in addition to the dollar was left murky by existing regulation and is what the Clarity Act is trying to address; today it is not permitted.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The single largest regulatory swing factor for issuer economics — legalizing on-chain yield would compete away the treasury spread that funds Circle and Tether's earnings.
insights.quote: the one thing that the regulation left pretty murky, which is what the Clarity Act is trying to uh address, is can you bring yield on chain

insights.claim: Because yield cannot be paid on-chain, Circle instead routes a huge portion of its treasury yield to Coinbase as a customer acquisition cost to get Coinbase members using USDC.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Distribution, not issuance, captures the economics — the party holding the customer relationship extracts the yield, which is the template for bank and network coin launches.
insights.quote: that's why you have these arrangements like they have with Coinbase where they're basically paying a huge portion of the yield to Coinbase as a customer acquisition cost

insights.claim: Nelson characterizes Circle as an on-chain money market account masked as a stablecoin, with a material counterparty-quality delta versus Tether driven by US regulatory footprint, 100% treasury backing and transparency into the trust account.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Treat stablecoin exposure as short-duration MMF credit risk and differentiate issuers on reserve transparency, not brand.
insights.quote: I view Circle as a onchain money market account in some ways, you know, kind of masked as a stable coin

insights.claim: A regulated stablecoin can theoretically break the buck the same way a money market fund can, but the mechanism would be panic rather than asset impairment, since the underlying reserves are at least as safe as traditional financial system assets.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The tail risk to underwrite is a run/confidence event, not collateral quality — watch redemption gates and reserve attestation cadence, not the asset mix.
insights.quote: theoretically, could you break the buck? Yes, in the same way that money market funds theoretically can make break the buck, which is just a function of panic

themes.theme: Distribution plays: Rain, Velocity and enterprise adoption

insights.claim: FirstMark portfolio company Rain is a stablecoin-backed card issuer and a principal Visa member, letting crypto exchanges and third parties offer cards spendable on the Visa network — solving the fact that most point-of-sale systems have no stablecoin integration.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The spend layer for stablecoins is being built on top of the card networks, not against them — a reason network volumes may benefit rather than erode near term.

insights.claim: Rain's customer base has migrated from crypto-native exchanges to digital-first neobanks and now to large US financial institutions, which Nelson presents as the template adoption curve for stablecoin infrastructure moving from niche to mainstream.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Customer-mix migration from crypto-native to regulated FIs is the leading indicator that a stablecoin infrastructure company has crossed into the real TAM.

insights.claim: Rain is growing as fast as any major AI company, according to Nelson — a growth benchmark that puts stablecoin payment infrastructure alongside AI as a private-market compounding category.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Suggests private capital allocation to stablecoin rails can compete with AI on growth, which should show up in valuations and eventual IPO supply.
insights.quote: that's a company that's growing, you know, as fast as any major AI company

insights.claim: FirstMark announced a Series A in Velocity, which sits on the merchant and acquirer side as a full-stack enterprise stablecoin solution — the mirror image of Rain's issuer-side business — because current stablecoin tooling is developer primitives that enterprises cannot assemble themselves.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: The bottleneck to enterprise stablecoin adoption is packaging, not technology — full-stack vendors capture the margin that developer-tool companies cannot.

insights.claim: A Series B fintech can stitch together stablecoin developer tools itself, but a Fortune 100 company coordinating treasury operations across 80 global markets cannot, creating the gap that full-stack enterprise providers are being funded to fill.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Enterprise treasury and cross-border FX is where the next dollar of stablecoin revenue lands; watch corporate treasurers' vendor selections as the adoption signal.
insights.quote: If you're a Fortune 100 company trying to think about how to combine uh treasury operations across 80 different global markets, like forget about it.

insights.claim: Nelson cites Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the Treasury Department expecting stablecoin issuance to reach three trillion dollars over the next five years, up from ~$300 billion today, with ancillary revenue in FX and B2B payments layered on top.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: A 10x issuance path implies roughly $3T of incremental treasury demand from issuers — a structural bid at the front end of the curve and a policy motive for supporting the sector.
insights.quote: what the uh Scott Besson uh and the Treasury Department expect will be three trillion in stable coin issuance over the next 5 years

themes.theme: AI agents settling on stablecoin rails

insights.claim: Nelson expects the vast majority of financial transactions to eventually be humans instructing an AI agent, with the agent needing an authenticated rail — and argues agents will not use wires or voice authorization, so the always-on programmable instant-settlement stablecoin layer becomes the default.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Frames agentic commerce as a demand driver for stablecoin volume; the rail that agents standardize on captures the transaction economics.

insights.claim: AI and stablecoins are complementary rather than competing platform shifts — AI generates the user interfaces and acts as the coordination layer for payments, while stablecoin rails deliver the value — but both are still early, in Nelson's analogy still in the grocery store rather than out of the jar.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Suggests the biggest fintech outcomes sit at the AI-plus-stablecoin intersection rather than in either category alone.
insights.quote: this is like peanut butter and jelly right now

insights.claim: Nelson's headline forecast is that in five to ten years the financial system will look entirely different, explicitly not tomorrow — a deliberately long-dated timeline for a shift he otherwise describes as already underway.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Calibrates the trade horizon: the thesis is a multi-year private-market compounding story, not a catalyst-driven public equity trade.
insights.quote: 5 10 years from now you're going to wake up and everything we know about the financial system is going to look uh entirely different

themes.theme: Tokenizing stocks and the end of the 9:30-to-4 market

insights.claim: The core case for tokenizing equities is not price discovery but operational: stocks trade roughly 8-to-5 instead of 24/7, collateral takes multiple days to settle instead of clearing immediately, and moving a position between brokers requires ACAT paperwork that tokenization eliminates.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Points the disruption at custody, clearing and transfer-agent intermediaries rather than at exchanges' matching engines.
insights.quote: right now stocks trade 85 instead of 247

insights.claim: Tokenization extends beyond equities to money market funds and bonds, where Nelson expects on-chain versions to deliver substantially more functionality — notably instant collateral delivery and lending without weeks of paperwork.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Collateral mobility is the killer app for RWA tokenization; watch prime brokerage and securities lending margins as the pressure point.

insights.claim: Dan Nathan counters that off-hours equity trading carries real risks — poor liquidity, limited transparency and unknown counterparties at, say, 3pm on a Saturday — even as he concedes most volume stays in normal hours and the risk is not material to most investors.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Execution quality in tokenized 24/7 venues is the underpriced risk; thin off-hours books are where retail gets adversely selected.

themes.theme: Hyperliquid, prediction markets and the everything-app for money

insights.claim: Hyperliquid, the largest perpetual-futures decentralized exchange, is about 80% of the size of Robinhood's crypto and equity businesses combined while running with roughly 12 employees.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: An offshore, 12-person venue at 80% of Robinhood's scale is a direct read on how much order flow US-regulated brokers are already ceding.
insights.quote: we we just looked it's about 80% of the size of uh Robin Hood if you combine their crypto and equity

insights.claim: IPO desks keep Hyperliquid open to manage pricing on pre-listing names, making perp DEXes a live price-discovery venue in the same way Kalshi and Polymarket became indicative for elections and geopolitical events.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Offshore perp and prediction venues are becoming reference prices for private assets and events — a free data feed for pre-IPO and event exposure.

insights.claim: Nelson argues US institutions cannot opt out of decentralized perp exchanges and prediction markets — nobody can turn Hyperliquid off — so the strategic question is KYC/AML integration rather than whether to participate.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Expect US brokers and regulators to move toward accommodation; the compliance-wrapper layer over offshore venues is an investable gap.
insights.quote: no one's turning Hyperliquid off and it's now almost as big as Robin Hood

insights.claim: Nelson expects sports betting, event contracts, equities and crypto to converge into single apps, so the durable moat for Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood and Wealthfront is brand affinity rather than product exclusivity.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Pure-play sports betting and prediction operators face funnel competition from funded brokerage accounts; bundling advantage favors Robinhood-style everything-apps.
insights.quote: why wouldn't your sports betting and your uh and your futures contract and your equity and your crypto all stay in one place?

insights.claim: Dan Nathan argues Robinhood's move to add event contracts and 24/7 sports betting on top of 27-28 million funded accounts was strategically brilliant because it monetizes an existing base that already enjoys moving assets around for pleasure.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Funded-account count is the asset; incremental product attach at near-zero CAC is the margin story to watch in Robinhood's numbers.

insights.claim: The entire fintech sector is less than 1% of global banking, stocks and brokerage, which Nelson uses as the sizing argument for why incremental share-taking from incumbents remains a massive profit pool.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Frames fintech penetration as a sub-1% starting point, arguing the sector's growth constraint is distribution and inertia rather than TAM.
insights.quote: the entire fintech sector is less than 1% of global banking and and uh and stocks and brokerage etc.

insights.claim: With hindsight, the correct 2023 fintech move was not to hunt new categories but to double and triple down on the winners built in the back half of the 2010s — Stripe, Revolute and emerging names like Ramp — which defined the value creation of the interim period.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: In a post-shift lull, concentration in proven category leaders beats new-category exploration — a reusable rule for allocating between cycles.
insights.quote: the thing to have done in, you know, 2023 was just to look at the winners who had been built in uh, you know, the back half of the 2010s and just continue to to double and triple down on them

insights.claim: Nelson's core venture framework is that returns are made by deploying at the platform-shift moment when there is an incontrovertible 'why now', and he says this is the first time in his venture career he has been positioned on the wave as it happens.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: Signals FirstMark is in aggressive deployment mode in fintech, implying rising private valuations and competition for stablecoin infrastructure deals.

insights.claim: Asked what the biggest risk to a public fintech portfolio is over one to three years, Nelson declines to answer as a public-markets investor and instead points to management teams as the determinant, because the game on the field is changing profoundly.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: In a platform shift, underwrite management adaptability over static competitive positioning — the differentiator is who can find and open the seam.
insights.quote: it all comes down to the person you're investing behind and the team that you're investing behind

insights.claim: Public fintech CEOs face a two-front problem: deciding their stablecoin and tokenization strategy for a shift that has not hit yet but will over the next five years, while simultaneously integrating AI, which Nelson frames as either a large revenue and cost benefit or the thing that kills them.
insights.speaker: Adam Nelson
insights.so_what: A screening lens for public fintech names: management teams with no articulated answer on both stablecoins and AI are the vulnerable cohort.
insights.quote: this might not have hit me yet, but it's about to hit me over the next 5 years when this stuff goes mainstream
